title: Burnishing polymer clay for a high-gloss finish
subtitle: Wet-sanding and buffing baked polymer clay to a mirror shine without varnish
excerpt: Polymer clay can be sanded through progressively finer grits and then buffed with a soft cloth or a rotary tool to produce a high-gloss finish that looks like glass. The process works on any baked polymer surface. No varnish needed and the shine does not yellow with age.
sourceNotes: Burnishing technique for polymer clay derived from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: A PVC-based modelling clay that cures hard in a domestic oven at 110-130°C
Polishing a surface by friction to produce a smooth, reflective finish

content.text: Burnishing
polymer clay

is a progressive wet-sanding process. The baked surface is scratched progressively finer until the scratches are too small to see, at which point the surface reflects light evenly. It produces a permanent polish that does not chip or yellow the way varnish does.
When to use this technique

Burnishing works on any baked polymer clay piece with a relatively smooth surface. Heavily textured pieces retain texture in the low points and can only be polished on the raised areas. Flat pendants, beads, and smooth cabochons give the best results.
What you need
Wet-and-dry sandpaper: 400 grit, 800 grit, 1200 grit, and 2000 grit
A bowl of water (for wet sanding)
A denim cloth or soft cotton cloth for final buffing
The baked polymer piece , fully cooled and hard
Step-by-step

Wet the 400-grit paper in the water bowl. Sand the polymer surface using circular strokes for 30 seconds per face. Keep the paper and surface wet throughout , dry sanding heats the polymer and creates deep scratches. The surface should look uniformly dull after this step.
Repeat with 800-grit wet paper. The surface should look less dull than after 400 grit. Sand until the deep scratches from 400 grit are replaced by the finer scratches of 800 grit.
Repeat with 1200-grit wet paper. The surface begins to show a slight sheen at this stage.
Repeat with 2000-grit wet paper. The surface should look near-gloss at this stage.

Dry the piece fully with a lint-free cloth. Rub the surface briskly with a denim cloth using firm pressure. The friction generates enough heat to bring the surface to a full gloss. Work in small circles for 30-60 seconds.
What the finish looks like when it is right

A properly burnished piece reflects a clear image, similar to lacquered wood or polished stone. There should be no visible scratches and no dull patches. Hold the piece under a light and tilt it , a fully polished surface shows the light source as a distinct highlight, not a diffuse glow.
Common mistakes
Skipping grits. Moving from 400 to 1200 directly leaves scratches from 400 that 1200 cannot remove. Each grit erases the previous grit's scratches.
Dry sanding. Dry abrasive generates friction heat that can warp thin polymer pieces. Use water throughout.
Buffing before sanding. Buffing at the denim step before the fine-grit sanding stages are complete produces a shiny piece with visible scratch patterns.
Pressing too hard with coarse grits. Aggressive pressure with 400 grit on cane-work or patterned pieces can sand through the surface layer and destroy the pattern.
